## Document project folder organization and index.cds in Jumpstart page

The "Jumpstart & Grow as You Go" guide needs a new section explaining how to organize project content beyond the default folder structure. Currently, the guide shows the default structure with `app/`, `srv/`, and `db/` folders, and explains how to override folder locations via `package.json` configuration. However, it doesn't explain how to organize files within subfolders when deviating from defaults.

Your task is to add a "Project Content" subsection to `get-started/jumpstart.md` that covers:

1. The **principle of locality** — related files should be placed next to each other (e.g., implementation logic as sibling files next to CDS service definitions). Include a link to the existing documentation about implementing services.
2. **Using subfolders** — explain that CAP assumes default locations for files, but when organizing specific file types (like annotation files or database-specific files) into subfolders, an `_index.cds_` file is required to tell CAP where to find them.

The section should be placed after the "Project Structure" section and before "Minimal Configuration". Use the appropriate heading levels (e.g., `### Project Content`) to match the existing document structure. Include a callout/tip box for the principle of locality as is common in this documentation.

## Environment Setup
This is a documentation repository built with VitePress. Check `package.json` for available scripts (e.g., `dev`, `build`, `docs:dev`). Review `.vitepress/config.ts` for site configuration and `CONTRIBUTING.md` for contribution guidelines and markdown conventions.

## Implementation Plan
- Locate the `get-started/jumpstart.md` file and review the current document flow around the "Project Structure" section.
    - Add a new `### Project Content` section between "Project Structure" and "Minimal Configuration".
    - Include a tip callout block explaining the principle of locality with a link to `/node.js/core-services#implementing-services`.
    - Add a `#### Using Subfolders` subsection explaining the need for `_index.cds_` files when organizing files into subfolders. Reference that CAP assumes defaults and index files are required to deviate from them.
    - Ensure the language matches the existing style — concise, convention-focused, and uses the existing terminology (e.g., "convention over configuration").
    - Verify the section renders correctly in the local VitePress dev server before submitting.

This also allows us to mock remote services in service integration scenarios. 233: 234: For example, assuming we want to integrate Business Partners from S/4, we do so by importing a service API, for example, the [EDMX from SAP Business Accelerator Hub](https://api.sap.com/api/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER), and translating it into a CDS service definition using `cds import`. 100: ## Implementing Services
101: 
102: By default `cds.serve` creates an instance of `cds.ApplicationService` for each service definition it finds. Each instance provides generic implementations for all CRUD operations, including full support for deep document structures, declarative input validation and many other out-of-the-box features. Yet, you'd likely need to provide domain-specific custom logic, especially for custom actions and functions, or for custom validations. In the next sections, you can learn the following:
103: 
104: - **How** to provide custom implementations?
105: - **Where**, that is, in which files, to add the implementation?
106: 
107: 
108: 
109: #### In sibling `.js` files, next to `.cds` sources
110: 
111: The easiest way to add custom service implementations is to simply place a `.js` file with the same name next to the `.cds` file containing the respective service definition. For example, as in [*cap/samples/bookshop*](https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-cap-samples/blob/main/bookshop/):
112: 
113: ```zsh
114: bookshop/
115: ├─ srv/
116: │ ├─ admin-service.cds
117: │ ├─ admin-service.js
118: │ ├─ cat-service.cds # [!code focus]
119: │ └─ cat-service.js # [!code focus]
120: └─ ...
121: ```
122: 
123: ::: details Alternatively in subfolders `lib/` or `handlers/`...
124: 
125:  In addition to adding the implementation in a neighbouring file you can place them in nested subfolders called `lib/` or `handlers/`, for example:

120: ### Project Structure
121: 
122: The default project structure of CAP projects is as follows:
123: 
124: ```zsh
125: bookshop/        # Your project's root folder
126: ├─ app/          # UI-related content
127: ├─ srv/          # Service-related content
128: ├─ db/           # Domain models and database-related content
129: ├─ package.json  # Configuration for cds + cds-dk
130: └─ readme.md     # A readme placeholder
131: ```
132: 
133: ### Project Content
134: 
135: Beyond the top-level folder structure, CAP doesn't assume a fixed mapping between folders and file types. You can organize content within folders as you like, for example, by placing related files into subfolders.
136: 
137: ::: tip Principle of Locality
138: 
139: Keep related files close together. For example, place custom service implementations as sibling files next to the CDS service definitions of the respective services. [Learn more about implementing services.](/node.js/core-services#implementing-services){.learn-more}
140: 
141: :::
142: 
143: #### Using Subfolders
144: 
145: While CAP assumes default locations for files, you can also organize specific file types into subfolders, for example, annotation files or database-specific files. When deviating from CAP's defaults like that, CAP expects to find an `index.cds` file in such subfolders, telling it which files to load from that folder.
146: 
147: 
148: 
149: ### Minimal Configuration
150: Following the [convention over configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_over_configuration) paradigm, CAP has defaults for many things that you'd have to configure in other frameworks. The goal is that things should just work out of the box, with zero configuration, whenever possible. You can override these defaults by specific configuration if you need to do so.
151: 
152: For example you could override the defaults for the project structure like that:
153: 
154: ::: code-group

156: ```jsonc [package.json]
157: { ...
158:   "cds": {
159:     "folders": {
160:        "db": "database/",
161:        "srv": "services/",
162:        "app": "uis/"
163:     }
164:   }
165: }
166: ```
167: 
168: :::
169:

171: 
172: We recommend to stay with CAP's conventions to benefit from things just working out of the box. Only add configuration or override the defaults if you really need to do so.

In case of `INSERT...as(SELECT...)`, the iterator returns `{}` for each row 42: - `affectedRows`: the number inserted (root) entries or the number of affectedRows in case of INSERT into SELECT 43: - `valueOf()`: returns `affectedRows` such that comparisons like `result > 0` can be used 44: ::: tip 45: `===` can't be used as it also compares the type 46: ::: 47: 48: 49: ## cds.DatabaseService — Configuration {#databaseservice-configuration } 50: [databaseservice configuration]: #databaseservice-configuration 51: 52: ### Pool 53: 54: Instead of opening and closing a database connection for every request, we use a pool to reuse connections. 55: By default, the following [pool configuration](https://www.npmjs.com/package/generic-pool) is used: 56: 57: ```json 58: { 59: "acquireTimeoutMillis": , 60: "evictionRunIntervalMillis": <2 * (idleTimeoutMillis || softIdleTimeoutMillis || 30000)>, 61: "min": 0, 62: "max": 100, 63: "numTestsPerEvictionRun": <(max - min) / 3>, 64: "softIdleTimeoutMillis": 30000, 65: "idleTimeoutMillis": 30000, 66: "testOnBorrow": true, 67: "fifo": false 68: } 69: ``` 70: 71: ::: warning 72: This default pool configuration does not apply to `@cap-js` database implementations. 73: ::: 74: 75: The _generic-pool_ has a built-in pool evictor, which inspects idle database connections in the pool and destroys them if they are too old. 76: 77: The following parameters are provided in the pool configuration: 78: 79: - _acquireTimeoutMillis_: The parameter specifies how much time it is allowed to wait an existing connection is fetched from the pool or a new connection is established. 80: - _evictionRunIntervalMillis_: The parameter specifies how often to run eviction checks. In case of 0 the check is not run. 81: - _min_: Minimum number of database connections to keep in pool at any given time. 82: ::: warning 83: This should be kept at the default 0. Otherwise every eviction run destroys all unused connections older than `idleTimeoutMillis` and afterwards creates new connections until `min` is reached. 84: ::: 85: 86: - _max_: Maximum number of database connections to keep in pool at any given time. 87: - _numTestsPerEvictionRun_: Number of database connections to be checked with one eviction run. 88: - _softIdleTimeoutMillis_: Amount of time database connection may sit idle in the pool before it is eligible for eviction. At least "min" connections should stay in the pool. In case of -1 no connection can get evicted. 89: - _idleTimeoutMillis_: The minimum amount of time that a database connection may stay idle in the pool before it is eligible for eviction due to idle time. 90: This parameter supercedes softIdleTimeoutMillis. 91: - _testOnBorrow_: Should the pool validate the database connections before giving them to the clients? 92: - _fifo_: If false, the most recently released resources will be the first to be allocated (stack). If true, the oldest resources will be first to be allocated (queue). Default value: false. 93: 94: Pool configuration can be adjusted by setting the `pool` option as shown in the following example: 95: 96: ```json 97: { 98: "cds": { 99: "requires": { 100: "db": { 101: "kind": "hana", 102: "pool": { 103: "acquireTimeoutMillis": 5000, 104: "min": 0, 105: "max": 100, 106: "fifo": true 107: } 108: } 109: } 110: } 111: } 112: ``` 113: 114: ::: warning _❗ Warning_ 115: The parameters are very specific to the current technical setup, such as the application environment and database location. 116: Even though we provide a default pool configuration, we expect that each application provides its own configuration based on its specific needs. 117: ::: 118: 119: 120: 121:

[Upsert](../cds/cqn.md#upsert) updates existing entity records from the given data or inserts new ones if they don't exist in the database. 131: 132: ::: warning 133: Even if an entity doesn't exist in the database:
→ Upsert is **not** equivalent to Insert. 134: ::: 135: 136: `UPSERT` statements can be created with the [UPSERT](cds-ql#upsert) query API: 137: 138: ```js 139: UPSERT.into('db.Books') 140: .entries({ ID: 4711, title: 'Wuthering Heights', stock: 100 }) 141: ``` 142: 143: `UPSERT` queries are translated into DB native upsert statements, more specifically they unfold to an [UPSERT SQL statement](https://help.sap.com/docs/HANA_CLOUD_DATABASE/c1d3f60099654ecfb3fe36ac93c121bb/ea8b6773be584203bcd99da76844c5ed.html) on SAP HANA and to an [INSERT ON CONFLICT SQL statement](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_upsert.html) on SQLite. 144: 145: - The rows to be upserted need to have the same structure, that is, all rows needs to specify the same named values. 146: - The upsert data must contain all key elements of the entity. 147: - If upsert data is incomplete only the given values are updated or inserted, which means the `UPSERT` statement has "PATCH semantics". 148: - `UPSERT` statements don't have a where clause. You can always use the basic configuration and override individual properties to create a different setup: 87: 88: 1. Install a database driver package, for example: 89: ```sh 90: npm add @cap-js/sqlite 91: ``` 92: 93: > Add option `-D` if you want this for development only. 94: 95: 2. Configure the primary database as a required service through `cds.requires.db`, for example: 96: 97: ```json 98: {"cds":{ 99: "requires": { 100: "db": { 101: "kind": "sqlite", 102: "impl": "@cap-js/sqlite", 103: "credentials": { 104: "url": "db.sqlite" 105: } 106: } 107: } 108: }} 109: ``` 110: 111: The config options are as follows: 112: 113: - `kind` — a name of a preset, like `sql`, `sqlite`, `postgres`, or `hana` 114: - `impl` — the module name of a CAP database service implementation 115: - `credentials` — an object with db-specific configurations, most commonly `url` 116: 117: ::: warning Don't configure credentials 118: 119: Credentials like `username` and `password` should **not** be added here but provided through service bindings, for example, via `cds bind`. 120: 121: ::: 122: 123: ::: tip Use `cds env` to inspect effective configuration 124: 125: For example, running this command: 126: 127: ```sh 128: cds env cds.requires.db 129: ``` 130: → prints: 131: 132: ```sh 133: { 134: kind: 'sqlite', 135: impl: '@cap-js/sqlite', 136: credentials: { url: 'db.sqlite' } 137: } 138: ``` 139: 140: ::: 141: 142:
143: 144: ### Built-in Database Support {.impl .java} 145: 146: CAP Java has built-in support for different SQL-based databases via JDBC. This section describes the different databases and any differences between them with respect to CAP features. There's out of the box support for SAP HANA with CAP currently as well as H2 and SQLite. However, it's important to note that H2 and SQLite aren't enterprise grade databases and are recommended for non-productive use like local development or CI tests only. PostgreSQL is supported in addition, but has various limitations in comparison to SAP HANA, most notably in the area of schema evolution. 147: 148: Database support is enabled by adding a Maven dependency to the JDBC driver, as shown in the following table: 149: 150: | Database | JDBC Driver | Remarks | 151: | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | 152: | **[SAP HANA Cloud](databases-hana)** | `com.sap.cloud.db.jdbc:ngdbc` | Recommended for productive use | 153: | **[H2](databases-h2)** | `com.h2database:h2` | Recommended for development and CI | 154: | **[SQLite](databases-sqlite)** | `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` | Supported for development and CI
Recommended for local MTX | 155: | **[PostgreSQL](databases-postgres)** | `org.postgresql:postgresql` | Supported for productive use | 156: 157: [Learn more about supported databases in CAP Java and their configuration](../java/cqn-services/persistence-services#database-support){ .learn-more} 158: 159: ## Providing Initial Data 160: 161: You can use CSV files to fill your database with initial data - see [Location of CSV Files](#location-of-csv-files). 162: 163:
164: 165: For example, in our [*cap/samples/bookshop*](https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-cap-samples/tree/main/bookshop/db/data) application, we do so for *Books*, *Authors*, and *Genres* as follows: 166: 167: ```zsh 168: bookshop/ 169: ├─ db/ 170: │ ├─ data/ # place your .csv files here 171: │ │ ├─ sap.capire.bookshop-Authors.csv 172: │ │ ├─ sap.capire.bookshop-Books.csv 173: │ │ ├─ sap.capire.bookshop-Books.texts.csv 174: │ │ └─ sap.capire.bookshop-Genres.csv 175: │ └─ schema.cds 176: └─ ... 177: ``` 178:
179: 180:
181: 182: For example, in our [CAP Samples for Java](https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-cap-samples-java/tree/main/db/data) application, we do so for some entities such as *Books*, *Authors*, and *Genres* as follows: 183: 184: ```zsh 185: db/ 186: ├─ data/ # place your .csv files here 187: │ ├─ my.bookshop-Authors.csv 188: │ ├─ my.bookshop-Books.csv 189: │ ├─ my.bookshop-Books.texts.csv 190: │ ├─ my.bookshop-Genres.csv 191: │ └─ ... 192: └─ index.cds 193: ``` 194:
195: 196: 197: The **filenames** are expected to match fully qualified names of respective entity definitions in your CDS models, optionally using a dash `-` instead of a dot `.` for cosmetic reasons. 198: 199: ### Using `.csv` Files 200: 201: The **content** of these files is standard CSV content with the column titles corresponding to declared element names, like for `Books`: 202: 203: ::: code-group 204: 205: ```csvc [db/data/sap.capire.bookshop-Books.csv] 206: ID,title,author_ID,stock 207: 201,Wuthering Heights,101,12 208: 207,Jane Eyre,107,11 209: 251,The Raven,150,333 210: 252,Eleonora,150,555 211: 271,Catweazle,170,22 212: ``` 213: 214: ::: 215: 216: > Note: `author_ID` is the generated foreign key for the managed Association `author` → learn more about that in the [Generating SQL DDL](#generating-sql-ddl) section. 217: 218: If your content contains ... 219: 220: - commas or line breaks → enclose it in double quotes `"..."` 221: - double quotes → escape them with doubled double quotes: `""...""` 222: 223: ```csvc 224: ID,title,descr 225: 252,Eleonora,"""Eleonora"" is a short story by Edgar Allan Poe, first published in 1842 in Philadelphia in the literary annual The Gift." 226: ``` 227: 228: ::: danger 229: On SAP HANA, only use CSV files for _configuration data_ that can't be changed by application users. 230: → See [CSV data gets overridden in the SAP HANA guide for details](databases-hana#csv-data-gets-overridden). 231: ::: 232: 233: ### Use `cds add data` 234: 235: Run this to generate an initial set of empty `.csv` files with header lines based on your CDS model: 236: 237: ```sh 238: cds add data 239: ``` 240: 241: ### Location of CSV Files 242: 243: CSV files can be located in the folders _db/data_ and _test/data_ as well as in any _data_ folder next to your CDS model files. 244: 245: ::: details Adding initial data next to your data model 246: The content of these 'co-located' `.cds` files actually doesn't matter, but they need to be included in your data model, through a `using` clause in another file for example. 247: ::: 248: 249: ::: details On SAP HANA ... 250: CSV and _hdbtabledata_ files located in the _src_ folder of your database module will be treated as native SAP HANA artifacts and deployed as they are. 251: ::: 252: 253: Quite frequently you need to distinguish between sample data and real initial data. CAP supports this by allowing you to provide initial data in two places: 254: 255:
256: 257: | Location | Deployed... | Purpose | 258: | ----------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | 259: | `db/data` | always | initial data for configurations, code lists, and similar | 260: | `test/data` | if not in production | sample data for tests and demos | 261: 262:

You can configure different sets of CSV files in different [Spring profiles](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/htmlsingle/#features.profiles). This configuration reads CSV data from `test/data` if the profile `test` is active: 267: 268: ::: code-group 269: 270: ```yaml [srv/src/main/resources/application.yaml] 271: --- 272: spring: 273: config.activate.on-profile: test 274: cds: 275: dataSource.csv.paths: 276: - test/data/** 277: ``` 278: 279: ::: 280:
281: 282: 283: 284: 285: 286: ## Querying at Runtime 287: 288: 289: 290: 291: Most queries to databases are constructed and executed from [generic event handlers of CRUD requests](providing-services#serving-crud), so quite frequently there's nothing to do. The following is for the remaining cases where you have to provide custom logic, and as part of it execute database queries. 292: 293: 294: 295: 296: ### DB-Agnostic Queries 297: 298:
299: 300: At runtime, we usually construct and execute queries using cds.ql APIs in a database-agnostic way. For example, queries like this are supported for all databases: 301: 302: ```js 303: SELECT.from (Authors, a => { 304: a.ID, a.name, a.books (b => { 305: b.ID, b.title 306: }) 307: }) 308: .where ({name:{like:'A%'}}) 309: .orderBy ('name') 310: ``` 311: 312:
313: 314:
315: 316: At runtime, we usually construct queries using the [CQL Query Builder API](../java/working-with-cql/query-api) in a database-agnostic way. For example, queries like this are supported for all databases: 317: 318: ```java 319: Select.from(AUTHOR) 320: .columns(a -> a.id(), a -> a.name(), 321: a -> a.books().expand(b -> b.id(), b.title())) 322: .where(a -> a.name().startWith("A")) 323: .orderBy(a -> a.name()); 324: ``` 325: 326:
327: 328: 329: 330: ### Native DB Queries 331: 332: If required you can also use native database features by executing native SQL queries: 333: 334:
335: 336: ```js 337: cds.db.run (`SELECT from sqlite_schema where name like ?`, name) 338: ``` 339:
340: 341:
342: 343: Use Spring's [JDBC Template](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/current/javadoc-api/org/springframework/jdbc/core/JdbcTemplate.html) to [leverage native database features](../java/cqn-services/persistence-services#jdbctemplate) as follows: 344: 345: ```java 346: @Autowired 347: JdbcTemplate db; 348: ... 349: db.queryForList("SELECT from sqlite_schema where name like ?", name); 350: ``` 351:
352: 353: ### Reading `LargeBinary` / BLOB {.impl .node} 354: 355: Formerly, `LargeBinary` elements (or BLOBs) were always returned as any other data type. Now, they are skipped from `SELECT *` queries. Yet, you can still enforce reading BLOBs by explicitly selecting them. Then the BLOB properties are returned as readable streams. 356: 357: ```js 358: SELECT.from(Books) //> [{ ID, title, ..., image1, image2 }] // [!code --] 359: SELECT.from(Books) //> [{ ID, title, ... }] 360: SELECT(['image1', 'image2']).from(Books) //> [{ image1, image2 }] // [!code --] 361: SELECT(['image1', 'image2']).from(Books) //> [{ image1: Readable, image2: Readable }] 362: ``` 363: 364: [Read more about custom streaming in Node.js.](../node.js/best-practices#custom-streaming-beta){.learn-more} 365: 366: 367: ## Generating DDL Files {#generating-sql-ddl} 368: 369:
370: 371: 372: When you run your server with `cds watch` during development, an in-memory database is bootstrapped automatically, with SQL DDL statements generated based on your CDS models. 373: 374: You can also do this manually with the CLI command `cds compile --to `. 375: 376:
377: 378:
379: 380: When you've created a CAP Java application with `cds init --add java` or with CAP Java's [Maven archetype](../java/developing-applications/building#the-maven-archetype), the Maven build invokes the CDS compiler to generate a `schema.sql` file for your target database. In the `default` profile (development mode), an in-memory database is [initialized by Spring](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/docs/current/reference/htmlsingle/#howto.data-initialization) and the schema is bootstrapped from the `schema.sql` file. 381: 382: [Learn more about adding an inital database schema.](../java/cqn-services/persistence-services#initial-database-schema){.learn-more} 383: 384:
385: 386: ### Using `cds compile` 387: 388: 389: For example, given these CDS models (derived from [*cap/samples/bookshop*](https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-cap-samples/tree/main/bookshop)): 390: 391: ::: code-group 392: 393: ```cds [db/schema.cds] 394: using { Currency } from '@sap/cds/common'; 395: namespace sap.capire.bookshop; 396: 397: entity Books { 398: key ID : UUID; 399: title : localized String; 400: descr : localized String; 401: author : Association to Authors; 402: price : { 403: amount : Decimal; 404: currency : Currency; 405: } 406: } 407: 408: entity Authors { 409: key ID : UUID; 410: name : String; 411: books : Association to many Books on books.author = $self; 412: } 413: ``` 414: ::: 415: ::: code-group 416: 417: ```cds [srv/cat-service.cds] 418: using { sap.capire.bookshop as my } from '../db/schema'; 419: service CatalogService { 420: entity ListOfBooks as projection on Books { 421: *, author.name as author 422: } 423: } 424: ``` 425: ::: 426: 427: 428: Generate an SQL DDL script by running this in the root directory containing both *.cds* files: 429: 430:
431: 432: 433: ```sh 434: cds compile srv/cat-service --to sql --dialect sqlite > schema.sql 435: ``` 436: 437: Output: 438: 439: ::: code-group 440: 441: ```sql [schema.sql] 442: CREATE TABLE sap_capire_bookshop_Books ( 443: ID NVARCHAR(36) NOT NULL, 444: title NVARCHAR(5000), 445: descr NVARCHAR(5000), 446: author_ID NVARCHAR(36), 447: price_amount DECIMAL, 448: price_currency_code NVARCHAR(3), 449: PRIMARY KEY(ID) 450: ); 451: 452: CREATE TABLE sap_capire_bookshop_Authors ( 453: ID NVARCHAR(36) NOT NULL, 454: name NVARCHAR(5000), 455: PRIMARY KEY(ID) 456: ); 457: 458: CREATE TABLE sap_common_Currencies ( 459: name NVARCHAR(255), 460: descr NVARCHAR(1000), 461: code NVARCHAR(3) NOT NULL, 462: symbol NVARCHAR(5), 463: minorUnit SMALLINT, 464: PRIMARY KEY(code) 465: ); 466: 467: CREATE TABLE sap_capire_bookshop_Books_texts ( 468: locale NVARCHAR(14) NOT NULL, 469: ID NVARCHAR(36) NOT NULL, 470: title NVARCHAR(5000), 471: descr NVARCHAR(5000), 472: PRIMARY KEY(locale, ID) 473: ); 474: 475: CREATE VIEW CatalogService_ListOfBooks AS SELECT 476: Books.ID, 477: Books.title, 478: Books.descr, 479: author.name AS author, 480: Books.price_amount, 481: Books.price_currency_code 482: FROM sap_capire_bookshop_Books AS Books 483: LEFT JOIN sap_capire_bookshop_Authors AS author 484: ON Books.author_ID = author.ID; 485: 486: --- some more technical views skipped ... 487: ``` 488: 489: ::: 490: 491:
492: 493: 494:
495: 496: ```sh 497: cds compile srv/cat-service --to sql > schema.sql 498: ``` 499: 500: Output: 501: 502: ::: code-group 503: 504: ```sql [schema.sql] 505: CREATE TABLE sap_capire_bookshop_Books ( 506: createdAt TIMESTAMP(7), 507: createdBy NVARCHAR(255), 508: modifiedAt TIMESTAMP(7), 509: modifiedBy NVARCHAR(255), 510: ID INTEGER NOT NULL, 511: title NVARCHAR(111), 512: descr NVARCHAR(1111), 513: author_ID INTEGER, 514: genre_ID INTEGER, 515: stock INTEGER, 516: price DECFLOAT, 517: currency_code NVARCHAR(3), 518: image BINARY LARGE OBJECT, 519: PRIMARY KEY(ID) 520: ); 553: 554: CREATE VIEW CatalogService_ListOfBooks AS SELECT 555: Books_0.createdAt, 556: Books_0.modifiedAt, 557: Books_0.ID, 558: Books_0.title, 559: Books_0.author, 560: Books_0.genre_ID, 561: Books_0.stock, 562: Books_0.price, 563: Books_0.currency_code, 564: Books_0.image 565: FROM CatalogService_Books AS Books_0; 566: CREATE VIEW CatalogService_ListOfBooks AS SELECT 567: Books.ID, 568: Books.title, 569: Books.descr, 570: author.name AS author, 571: Books.price_amount, 572: Books.price_currency_code 573: FROM sap_capire_bookshop_Books AS Books 574: LEFT JOIN sap_capire_bookshop_Authors AS author 575: ON Books.author_ID = author.ID; 576: 577: --- some more technical views skipped ... 578: ``` 579: 580: ::: 581: 582:
583: 584: ::: tip 585: Use the specific SQL dialect (`hana`, `sqlite`, `h2`, `postgres`) with `cds compile --to sql --dialect ` to get DDL that matches the target database. 586: ::: 587: 588: 589: ### Rules for Generated DDL 590: 591: A few observations on the generated SQL DDL output: 592: 593: 1. **Tables / Views** — Declared entities become tables, projected entities become views. 594: 2. **Type Mapping** — [CDS types are mapped to database-specific SQL types](../cds/types). 595: 3. **Slugified FQNs** — Dots in fully qualified CDS names become underscores in SQL names. 596: 4. **Flattened Structs** — Structured elements like `Books:price` are flattened with underscores. 597: 5. **Generated Foreign Keys** — For managed to-one Associations, foreign key columns are created. For example, this applies to `Books:author`. 598: 599: 600: 601: 602: 603: In addition, you can use the following annotations to fine-tune generated SQL. 604: 605: 606: 607: ### @cds.persistence.skip 608: 609: Add `@cds.persistence.skip` to an entity to indicate that this entity should be skipped from generated DDL scripts, and also no SQL views to be generated on top of it: 610: 611: ```cds 612: @cds.persistence.skip 613: entity Foo {...} //> No SQL table will be generated 614: entity Bar as select from Foo; //> No SQL view will be generated 615: ``` 616: 617: 618: 619: ### @cds.persistence.exists 620: 621: Add `@cds.persistence.exists` to an entity to indicate that this entity should be skipped from generated DDL scripts. In contrast to `@cds.persistence.skip` a database relation is expected to exist, so we can generate SQL views on top. 622: 623: ```cds 624: @cds.persistence.exists 625: entity Foo {...} //> No SQL table will be generated 626: entity Bar as select from Foo; //> The SQL view will be generated 627: ``` 628: 629: ::: details On SAP HANA ... 630: 631: If the respective entity is a user-defined function or a calculation view, one of the annotations `@cds.persistence.udf` or `@cds.persistence.calcview` also needs to be assigned. See [Calculated Views and User-Defined Functions](../advanced/hana#calculated-views-and-user-defined-functions) for more details. 632: 633: ::: 634: 635: 636: 637: ### @cds.persistence.table 638: 639: Annotate an entity with `@cds.persistence.table` to create a table with the effective signature of the view definition instead of an SQL view. 640: 641: ```cds 642: @cds.persistence.table 643: entity Foo as projection on Bar {...} 644: ``` 645: 646: > All parts of the view definition not relevant for the signature (like `where`, `group by`, ...) are ignored. 647: 648: Use case for this annotation: Use projections on imported APIs as replica cache tables. 649: 650: 651: 652: ### @sql.prepend / append 653: 654: Use `@sql.prepend` and `@sql.append` to add native SQL clauses to before or after generated SQL output of CDS entities or elements. 655: 656: Example: 657: 658: ````cds 659: @sql.append: ```sql 660: GROUP TYPE foo 661: GROUP SUBTYPE bar 662: ``` 663: entity E { ..., 664: @sql.append: 'FUZZY SEARCH INDEX ON' 665: text: String(100); 666: } 667: 668: @sql.append: 'WITH DDL ONLY' 669: entity V as select from E { ... }; 670: ```` 671: 672: Output: 673: 674: ```sql 675: CREATE TABLE E ( ..., 676: text NVARCHAR(100) FUZZY SEARCH INDEX ON 677: ) GROUP TYPE foo 678: GROUP SUBTYPE bar; 679: 680: CREATE VIEW V AS SELECT ... FROM E WITH DDL ONLY; 681: ``` 682: 683: The following rules apply: 684: 685: - The value of the annotation must be a [string literal](../cds/cdl#multiline-literals). 686: 687: - The compiler doesn't check or process the provided SQL snippets in any way. You're responsible to ensure that the resulting statement is valid and doesn't negatively impact your database or your application. We don't provide support for problems caused by using this feature. 688: 689: - If you refer to a column name in the annotation, you need to take care of 690: a potential name mapping yourself, for example, for structured elements. 691: 692: - Annotation `@sql.prepend` is only supported for entities translating to tables. It can't be used with views nor with elements. 693: - For SAP HANA tables, there's an implicit that is overwritten by an explicitly provided `@sql.prepend`. 694: 695: * Both `@sql.prepend` and `@sql.append` are disallowed in SaaS extension projects. 696: 697: If you use native database clauses in combination with `@cds.persistence.journal`, see [Schema Evolution Support of Native Database Clauses](databases-hana#schema-evolution-native-db-clauses). 698: 699: 700: ### Reserved Words 701: 702: The CDS compiler and CAP runtimes provide smart quoting for reserved words in SQLite and in SAP HANA so that they can still be used in most situations. But in general reserved words cannot be used as identifiers. The list of reserved words varies per database. 703: 704: Find here a collection of resources on selected databases and their reference documentation: 705: 706: * [SAP HANA SQL Reference Guide for SAP HANA Platform (Cloud Version)](https://help.sap.com/docs/HANA_SERVICE_CF/7c78579ce9b14a669c1f3295b0d8ca16/28bcd6af3eb6437892719f7c27a8a285.html) 707: * [SAP HANA SQL Reference Guide for SAP HANA Cloud](https://help.sap.com/docs/HANA_CLOUD_DATABASE/c1d3f60099654ecfb3fe36ac93c121bb/28bcd6af3eb6437892719f7c27a8a285.html) 708: * [SQLite Keywords](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_keywords.html) 709: * [H2 Keywords/Reserved Words](https://www.h2database.com/html/advanced.html#keywords) 710: * [PostgreSQL SQL Key Words](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-keywords-appendix.html) 711: 712: [There are also reserved words related to SAP Fiori.](../advanced/fiori#reserved-words){.learn-more} 713: 714: 715: 716: 717: 718: ## Database Constraints {#db-constraints} 719: 720: The information about foreign key relations contained in the associations of CDS models can be used to generate foreign key constraints on the database tables. Within CAP, referential consistency is established only at commit. The ["deferred" concept for foreign key constraints](https://www.sqlite.org/foreignkeys.html) in SQL databases allows the constraints to be checked and enforced at the time of the [COMMIT statement within a transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html) rather than immediately when the data is modified, providing more flexibility in maintaining data integrity. 721: 722: Enable generation of foreign key constraints on the database with: 723: 724: ```js 725: cds.features.assert_integrity = 'db' 726: ``` 727: 728: ::: warning Database constraints are not supported for H2 729: Referential constraints on H2 cannot be defined as "deferred", which is needed for database constraints within CAP. 730: ::: 731: 732: With that switched on, foreign key constraints are generated for managed to-one associations. For example, given this model: 733: 734: ```cds 735: entity Books { 736: key ID : Integer; ... 737: author : Association to Authors; 738: } 739: entity Authors { 740: key ID : Integer; ... 741: } 742: ``` 743: 744: The following `Books_author` constraint would be added to table `Books`: 745: 746: ```sql 747: CREATE TABLE Authors ( 748: ID INTEGER NOT NULL, -- primary key referenced by the constraint 749: ..., 750: PRIMARY KEY(ID) 751: ); 752: CREATE TABLE Books ( 753: ID INTEGER NOT NULL, 754: author_ID INTEGER, -- generated foreign key field 755: ..., 756: PRIMARY KEY(ID), 757: CONSTRAINT Books_author -- constraint is explicitly named // [!code focus] 758: FOREIGN KEY(author_ID) -- link generated foreign key field author_ID ... 759: REFERENCES Authors(ID) -- ... with primary key field ID of table Authors 760: ON UPDATE RESTRICT 761: ON DELETE RESTRICT 762: VALIDATED -- validate existing entries when constraint is created 763: ENFORCED -- validate changes by insert/update/delete 764: INITIALLY DEFERRED -- validate only at commit 765: ) 766: ``` 767: 768: No constraints are generated for... 769: * Unmanaged associations or compositions 770: * To-many associations or compositions 771: * Associations annotated with `@assert.integrity: false` 772: * Associations where the source or target entity is annotated with `@cds.persistence.exists` or `@cds.persistence.skip` 773: 774: If the association is the backlink of a **composition**, the constraint's delete rule changes to `CASCADE`. 775: That applies, for example, to the `parent` association in here: 776: 777: ```cds 778: entity Genres { 779: key ID : Integer; 780: parent : Association to Genres; 781: children : Composition of many Genres on children.parent = $self; 782: } 783: ``` 784: 785: As a special case, a referential constraint with `delete cascade` is also generated 786: for the text table of a [localized entity](../guides/localized-data#localized-data), 787: although no managed association is present in the `texts` entity. 788: 789: Add a localized element to entity `Books` from the previous example: 790: ```cds 791: entity Books { 792: key ID : Integer; ... 793: title : localized String; 794: } 795: ``` 796: 797: The generated text table then is: 798: ```sql 799: CREATE TABLE Books_texts ( 800: locale NVARCHAR(14) NOT NULL, 801: ID INTEGER NOT NULL, 802: title NVARCHAR(5000), 803: PRIMARY KEY(locale, ID), 804: CONSTRAINT Books_texts_texts // [!code focus] 805: FOREIGN KEY(ID) 806: REFERENCES Books(ID) 807: ON UPDATE RESTRICT 808: ON DELETE CASCADE 809: VALIDATED 810: ENFORCED 811: INITIALLY DEFERRED 812: ) 813: ``` 814: 815: ::: warning Database constraints aren't intended for checking user input 816: Instead, they protect the integrity of your data in the database layer against programming errors. +The following sections give a brief overview of CAP's core concepts.
+
+### Service-Centric Paradigm
+
+A CAP application commonly provides services defined in CDS models and served by the CAP runtimes. Every active thing in CAP is a service. They embody the behavioral aspects of a domain in terms of exposed entities, actions, and events.
+
+![This graphic is explained in the accompanying text.](assets/providing-services/service-centric-paradigm.drawio.svg)
+
+### Ubiquitous Events
+
+At runtime, everything happening is in response to events. CAP features a ubiquitous notion of events, which represent both, *requests* coming in through **synchronous** APIs, as well as **asynchronous** *event messages*, blurring the line between both worlds.
+
+![This graphic shows that consumers send events to services and that there are hooks, so that event handlers can react on those events.](assets/providing-services/services-events.drawio.svg)
+
+### Event Handlers
+
+Service providers basically react on events in event handlers, plugged in to respective hooks provided by the core service runtimes.
+
+

1076: ### Expressions as Annotation Values <Beta /> {#expressions-as-annotation-values}
1077: 
1078: In order to use an expression as an annotation value, it must be enclosed in parentheses:
1079: ```cds
1080: @anExpression: ( foo.bar * 11 )
1081: ```
1082: 
1083: Syntactically, the same expressions are supported as in a select item or in the where clause of a query,
1084: except subqueries. The expression can of course also be a single reference or a simple value:
1085: ```cds
1086: @aRefExpr: ( foo.bar )
1087: @aValueExpr: ( 11 )
1088: ```
1089: 
1090: Some advantages of using expressions as "first class" annotation values are:
1091: * syntax and references are checked by the compiler
1092: * code completion
1093: * [automatic path rewriting in propagated annotations](#propagation)
1094: * [automatic translation of expressions in OData annotations](#odata-annotations)
1095: 
1096: ::: info Limitations
1097: Elements that are not available to the compiler, for example the OData draft decoration, can't be used in annotation expressions.
1098: :::
1099: 
1100: #### Name resolution
1101: 
1102: Each path in the expression is checked:
1103: * For an annotation assigned to an entity, the first path step is resolved as element of the entity.
1104: * For an annotation assigned to an entity element, the first path step is resolved as the annotated element or its siblings.
1105: * If the annotation is assigned to a subelement of a structured element, the top level
1106:   elements of the entity can be accessed via `$self`.
1107: * A parameter `par` can be accessed via `:par`, just like parameters of a parametrized entity in queries.
1108: * For an annotation assigned to a bound action or function, elements of the respective entity
1109:   can be accessed via `$self`.
1110: * The draft specific element `IsActiveEntity` can be referred to with the magic variable `$draft.IsActiveEntity`.
1111:   During draft augmentation `$draft.IsActiveEntity` is rewritten to `$self.IsActiveEntity` for all draft enabled
1112:   entities (root and sub nodes but not for named types or entity parameters).
1113: * If a path can't be resolved successfully, compilation fails with an error.
1114: 
1115: In contrast to `@aReference: foo.bar`, a single reference written as expression `@aRefExpr: ( foo.bar )`
1116: is checked by the compiler.

1118: ```cds
1119: @MyAnno: (a)            // reference to element
1120: entity Foo (par: Integer) {
1121:   key ID : Integer;
1122:   @MyAnno: (:par)       // reference to entity parameter
1123:   a : Integer;
1124:   @MyAnno: (a)          // reference to sibling element
1125:   b : Integer;
1126:   s {
1127:     @MyAnno: (y)        // reference to sibling element
1128:     x : Integer;
1129:     @MyAnno: ($self.a)  // reference to top level element
1130:     y : Integer;
1131:   }
1132: }
1133: actions {
1134:   @MyAnno: ($self.a)

1136: }
1137: ```

1141: In CSN, the expression is represented as a record with two properties:
1142: * A string representation of the expression is stored in property `=`.
1143: * A tokenized representation of the expression is stored in one of the properties

1146: ```json
1147: {
1148:   "@anExpression": {
1149:     "=": "foo.bar * 11",
1150:     "xpr": [ {"ref": ["foo", "bar"]}, "*", {"value": 11} ]
1151:   },
1152:   "@aRefExpr": {
1153:     "=": "foo.bar",
1154:     "ref": ["foo", "bar"]
1155:   },
1156:   "@aValueExpr": {
1157:     "=": "11",
1158:     "val": 11
1159:   }
1160: }
1161: ```

1163: Note the different CSN representations for a [plain value](#annotation-values) `"@anInteger": 11`
1164: and a value written as expression `@aValueExpr: ( 11 )`, respectively.

1166: #### Propagation
1167: 
1168: [Annotations are propagated](#annotation-propagation) in views/projections, via includes, and along type references.
1169: If the annotation value is an expression, it sometimes is necessary to adapt references inside the expression
1170: during propagation, for example, when a referenced element is renamed in a projection.
1171: The compiler automatically takes care of the necessary rewriting. When a reference in an annotation expression
1172: is rewritten, the `=` property is set to `true`.
1173: 
1174: Example:
1175: ```cds
1176: entity E {
1177:   @Common.Text: (text)
1178:   code : Integer;
1179:   text : String;
1180: }
1181: 
1182: entity P as projection on E {
1183:   code,
1184:   text as descr
1185: }
1186: ```
1187: When propagated to element `code` of projection `P`, the annotation is automatically
1188: rewritten to `@Common.Text: (descr)`.
1189: 
1190: ::: details Resulting CSN
1191: ```jsonc
1192: {
1193:   "definitions": {
1194:     "E": {  // ...
1195:       "elements": {  // ...
1196:         "code": {
1197:           // original annotation
1198:           "@Common.Text": { "=": "text",
1199:                             "ref": ["text"] },
1200:           "type": "cds.Integer"
1201:         },
1202:         "text": {"type": "cds.String"}
1203:       }
1204:     },
1205:     "P": {  // ...
1206:       "elements": {  // ...
1207:         "code": {
1208:           // propagated annotation, reference adapted
1209:           "@Common.Text": { "=": true,
1210:                             "ref": ["descr"] },
1211:           "type": "cds.Integer"
1212:         },
1213:         "descr": {"type": "cds.String"}
1214:       }
1215: } } }

1750: #### Bound Actions and Functions { #bound-actions}
1751: 
1752: Actions and functions can also be bound to individual entities of a service, enclosed in an additional `actions` block as the last clause in an entity/view definition.
1753: 
1754: ```cds
1755: service CatalogService {
1756:   entity Products as projection on data.Products { ... }
1757:     actions {
1758:       // bound actions/functions
1759:       action addRating (stars: Integer);
1760:       function getViewsCount() returns Integer;
1761:     }
1762: }
1763: ```
1764: 
1765: Bound actions and functions have a binding parameter that is usually implicit.
1766: It can also be modeled explicitly: the first parameter of a bound action or function is treated as binding parameter,
1767: if it's typed by `[many] $self`. Use Explicit Binding to control the naming of the binding parameter. Use the
1768: keyword `many` to indicate that the action or function is bound to a collection of instances rather than to a single one.
1769: 
1770: ```cds
1771: service CatalogService {
1772:   entity Products as projection on data.Products { ... }
1773:     actions {
1774:       // bound actions/functions with explicit binding parameter
1775:       action A1 (prod: $self, stars: Integer);
1776:       action A2 (in: many $self);  // bound to collection of Products
1777:     }
1778: }
1779: ```
1780: 
1781: Explicitly modelled binding parameters are ignored for OData V2.
1782: 
1783: 
1784: ### Custom-Defined Events {#events}
1785: 
1786: Similar to [Actions and Functions](../cds/cdl#actions) you can declare `events`, which a service emits via messaging channels. Essentially, an event declaration looks very much like a type definition, specifying the event's name and the type structure of the event messages' payload.
1787: 
1788: ```cds
1789: service MyOrders { ...
1790:   event OrderCanceled {
1791:     orderID: Integer;
1792:     reason: String;
1793:   }
1794: }
1795: ```
1796: 
1797: An event can also be defined as projection on an entity, type, or another event.
1798: Only the effective signature of the projection is relevant.
1799: ```cds
1800: service MyOrders { ...
1801:   event OrderCanceledNarrow : projection on OrderCanceled { orderID }
1802: }
1803: ```
1804: 
1805: 
1806: ### Extending Services {#extend-service}
1807: 
1808: You can [extend](#extend) services with additional entities and actions much as you would add new entities to a context:
1809: 
1810: ```cds
1811: extend service CatalogService with {
1812:   entity Foo {};
1813:   function getRatings() returns Integer;
1814: }
1815: ```
1816: 
1817: Similarly, you can [extend](#extend) entities with additional actions
1818: as you would add new elements:
1819: 
1820: 
1821: ```cds
1822: extend entity CatalogService.Products with actions {
1823:   function getRatings() returns Integer;
1824: }
1825: ```

conversation.content:
name: Lint

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - '**.md'
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  suggestions:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: '! github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork'
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
    - name: Checkout SAP repo
      run: |
        git config --global credential.helper "cache --timeout=3600"
        echo -e "url=https://user:${GH_TOKEN}@github.com\n" | git credential approve
        echo -e "url=https://user:${GH_TOKEN_PARENT}@github.tools.sap\n" | git credential approve
        git clone --depth 1 --no-single-branch https://github.tools.sap/cap/docs docs
        cd docs
        git checkout $GITHUB_HEAD_REF || git checkout main
        git submodule update --init --recursive
        cd @external
        git checkout $GITHUB_HEAD_REF
      env:
        GH_TOKEN:        ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        GH_TOKEN_PARENT: ${{ secrets.GH_TOKEN_PARENT }}
    - name: Use Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: 18.x
        cache: 'npm'
        cache-dependency-path: docs/package-lock.json
    - run: npm ci
      working-directory: docs
    - run: git checkout ${{ github.head_ref }}
      working-directory: docs/@external
    - name: Get changes
      id: changes
      working-directory: docs/@external
      run: |
        echo "DIFF_FILES=$(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRT ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} -- '*.md' | xargs)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    - name: Run cspell
      if: steps.changes.outputs.DIFF_FILES != ''
      id: cspell
      continue-on-error: true
      working-directory: docs/@external
      run: |
        npx cspell --no-progress --show-suggestions --show-context ${{ steps.changes.outputs.DIFF_FILES }} >> ${{ github.workspace }}/docs/@external/CSPELL.log
    - name: Run markdownlint
      if: steps.changes.outputs.DIFF_FILES != ''
      id: markdownlint
      continue-on-error: true
      working-directory: docs/@external
      run: |
        npx markdownlint-cli --output ${{ github.workspace }}/docs/@external/MARKDOWNLINT.log -r markdownlint-rule-search-replace ${{ steps.changes.outputs.DIFF_FILES }}
    - name: Create review
      id: create_review
      if: steps.cspell.outcome == 'failure' || steps.markdownlint.outcome == 'failure'
      uses: actions/github-script@v6
      env:
        SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
        BASE_DIR: ${{ github.workspace }}/docs/@external
        BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        PULL_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.number }}
        HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
        REPO: 'docs'
        REPO_OWNER: 'cap-js'
      with:
        script: |
          const script = require('${{ github.workspace }}/docs/@external/.github/etc/create-review.cjs')
          await script({github, context, core, require, exec})
---
---
$schema: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/streetsidesoftware/cspell/main/cspell.schema.json
version: '0.2'
language: en-US,en-GB
dictionaryDefinitions:
  - name: project-words-internal
    path: '../project-words.txt'
    addWords: true
  - name: project-words-external
    path: './project-words.txt'
    addWords: true
dictionaries:
  - project-words-internal
  - project-words-external
  - companies
  - softwareTerms
  - misc
  - node
  - typescript
  - bash
  - html
  - css
ignorePaths:
  - 'node_modules'
  - 'project-words.txt'
  - '.github'
allowCompoundWords: true
caseSensitive: false
ignoreRegExpList:
  - code_block
  - inline_code_block
  - code-group
  - href_link
  - markdown_link
  - fragments
  - html_comment
  - heading
  - heading_ids
  - bold_text
  - italic_text
  - i_tags
  - cli_option
  - property
  - property_in_code_block
patterns:
  - name: code_block
    pattern: /`{3}[\s\S]*?`{3}/gm

  - name: inline_code_block
    pattern: /\`[-.]?[\s\S]*?(?!\w)\`/gm

  - name: html_comment
    pattern: /<!--[\s\S]*?-->/gm

  - name: markdown_link

74:    </dependency>

13: # no-java-keywords
14: 
15: ## Rule Details
16: 
17: The CAP Java code generation bases its class and method names on CDS entities.
18: If reserved Java keywords are used as CDS identifiers, the code generation or compilation may fail.
19: This rule helps identify such identifiers early on and suggest to use the `@cds.java.name` annotation.
20: 
21: ## Examples
22: 
23: #### ✅   Correct example
24: 
25: In the following example, use of the reserved Java keyword as identifiers is fixed via the `@cds.java.name` annotation, so the rule doesn't raise any warnings:

30: <PlaygroundBadge

32:   kind="correct"

34:   :files="['db/schema.cds']"
35:   :packages="{'cds': { 'requires': {'db': { 'kind': 'sql' } }} }"
36: />
37: 
38: #### ❌   Incorrect example

13: # auth-restrict-grant-service
14: 
15: ## Rule Details
16: 
17: Restrictions can be defined on different types of CDS resources, but there are some limitations with regard to supported privileges (see [limitations](../../../guides/security/authorization#supported-combinations-with-cds-resources)).
18: 
19: Unsupported privilege properties are ignored by the runtime. Especially, for bound or unbound actions, the `grant` property is implicitly removed (assuming `grant: '*'` instead). The same is true for functions. This rule ensures that `@restrict.grant` on service level and for bound/unbound actions and functions is limited to `grant: '*'`.
20: 
21: ## Examples
22: 
23: #### ✅   Correct example
24: 
25: Let's consider the following example with the `CatalogService` where the function `getViewsCount()` is restricted to the *Admin* role, granting all CDS events:
26: 
27: ::: code-group
28: <<< ../examples/auth-restrict-grant-service/correct/srv/cat-service.cds#snippet{cds:line-numbers} [srv/cat-service.cds]
29: :::
30: <PlaygroundBadge
31:   name="auth-restrict-grant-service"
32:   kind="correct"
33:   :rules="{'@sap/cds/auth-restrict-grant-service': ['error', 'show']}"
34:   :files="['srv/cat-service.cds', 'db/schema.cds']"
35: />
36: 
37: #### ❌   Incorrect example
38: 
39: If we were to slightly modify the above example and use `grant: ['WRITE']` in the privilege of the function, the rule would be
40: triggered to inform us that the value of `grant` is limited to `'*'`:
41: 
42: ::: code-group
43: <<< ../examples/auth-restrict-grant-service/incorrect/srv/cat-service.cds#snippet{cds:line-numbers} [srv/cat-service.cds]
44: :::
45: <PlaygroundBadge
46:   name="auth-restrict-grant-service"
47:   kind="incorrect"
48:   :rules="{'@sap/cds/auth-restrict-grant-service': ['error', 'show']}"
49:   :files="['srv/cat-service.cds', 'db/schema.cds']"
50: />
51: 
52: ## Version
53: This rule was introduced in `@sap/eslint-plugin-cds 2.6.4`.

# no-db-keywords

## Rule Details

The CDS compiler and CAP runtimes provide smart quoting for reserved words in SQLite so that they can still be used in most situations.
But in general reserved words cannot be used as identifiers and this rule warns you if you use any of the [reserved SQL keywords](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_keywords.html).

## Examples

#### ✅   Correct example

In the following example, none of the reserved SQL keywords are used as identifiers, so the rule doesn't raise any warnings:

::: code-group
<<< ../examples/no-db-keywords/correct/db/schema.cds#snippet{cds:line-numbers} [db/schema.cds]
:::
<PlaygroundBadge
  name="no-db-keywords"
  kind="correct"
  :rules="{'@sap/cds/no-db-keywords': ['warn', 'show']}"
  :files="['db/schema.cds']"
  :packages="{'cds': { 'requires': {'db': { 'kind': 'sql' } } } }"
/>

#### ❌   Incorrect example

In the next example, the reserved SQL keyword `Order` is used as an entity name, so the rule will raise a warning:
<!-- TODO: Remove devDependency as soon as rule fix is released -->

<<< ../examples/no-db-keywords/incorrect/db/schema.cds#snippet{cds:line-numbers} [db/schema.cds]

  kind="incorrect"
  :rules="{'@sap/cds/no-db-keywords': ['warn', 'show']}"
  :files="['db/schema.cds']"
  :packages="{'devDependencies': { '@cap-js/sqlite': '^1' } }"
/>

## Version
This rule was introduced in `@sap/eslint-plugin-cds 2.1.0`.

## Rule Details

With compiler v2, appending a type declaration to a column expression in a view's query doesn't generate a cast in SQL anymore, as that created conflicts with various database-specific behaviors. This rule ensures that such casts are added explicitly by suggesting possible missing SQL casts.

CAP provides intrinsic extensibility, which means all your entities and services are extensible by default.
Your SaaS app becomes the base app for extensions by your customers, and your data model the base model. Normally,

Restrictions can be defined on different types of CDS resources, but there are some limitations with regard to supported privileges (see [limitations](../../../guides/security/authorization#supported-combinations-with-cds-resources)).

45: For example given we have to handle input like this:
46: ```js

48: ```
49:

53: try {
54:   uri = decodeURI(input)
55: } catch {

57: }
58: ```

64: ```

68: ### local (*filename*) {.method}
69: 
70: Returns a relative representation of `filename` to the original `process.cwd()`.
71: 
72: We commonly use that in CAP implementations to print filenames to stdout that you can click to open, for example in VS Code terminal output, regardless from where you started your server.
73: 
74: For example, if we run bookshop from the parent folder, filenames are correctly printed with a `bookshop/` prefix:
75: 
76: ```log
77: [samples] cds run bookshop
78: [cds] - loaded model from 5 file(s):
79: 
80:   bookshop/srv/user-service.cds
81:   bookshop/srv/cat-service.cds
82:   bookshop/srv/admin-service.cds
83:   bookshop/db/schema.cds
84: ...
85: ```
86: 
87: If we run it from within the *bookshop* folder, no prefixes show up:
88: 
89: ```log
90: [bookshop] cds run

92: 
93:   srv/user-service.cds
94:   srv/cat-service.cds
95:   srv/admin-service.cds
96:   db/schema.cds
97: ...
98: ```

102: ### exists (*file*) {.method}
103: 
104: Checks if a given file or folder exists; `file` is resolved relative to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).
105: 
106: ```js
107: const { exists } = cds.utils
108: if (exists('server.js')) // ...
109: ```
110: 
111: Basically the implementation looks like that:
112: 
113: ```js
114: if (file) return fs.existsSync (path.resolve (cds.root,file))
115: ```
116: 
117: 
118: 
119: ### isdir (*file*) {.method}
120: 
121: Checks if the given filename refers to an existing directory, and returns the fully resolved absolute filename, if so.
122: 
123: ```js
124: const { isdir, fs } = cds.utils
125: let dir = isdir ('app')
126: if (dir) {
127:    let entries = fs.readdirSync(dir)
128:    ...
129: }
130: ```
131: 
132: Returns `undefined` or a fully resolved absolute filename of the existing directory, including recursively resolving symbolic links. Relative fileames are resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root),
133: 
134: 
135: 
136: ### isfile (*file*) {.method}
137: 
138: Checks if the given filename pints to an existing file, and returns the fully resolved absolute filename, if so.
139: 
140: ```js
141: const { isfile, fs } = cds.utils
142: let file = isdir ('package.json')
143: let json = fs.readFileSync (file,'utf8')
144: ```
145: 
146: Returns `undefined` or a fully resolved absolute filename of the existing directory, including recursively resolving symbolic links. Relative fileames are resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root),
147: 
148: 
149: 
150: ### async read (*file*) {.method}
151: 
152: Reads content of the given file.
153: 
154: ```js
155: const { read } = cds.utils
156: let pkg = await read ('package.json')
157: ```
158: 
159: Relative fileames are resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root). The implementation uses `utf8` encoding by default. If the file is a `.json` file, the read content is automatically `JSON.parse`d.
160: 
161: 
162: 
163: ### async write (*data*) .to (...*file*) {.method}
164: 
165: Writes content to a given file, optionally with a fluent API.
166: 
167: ```js
168: const { write } = cds.utils
169: await write ({foo:'bar'}) .to ('some','file.json')
170: await write ({foo:'bar'}) .to ('some/file.json')
171: await write ('some/file.json', {foo:'bar'})
172: ```
173: 
174: Relative fileames are resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root). If provided data is an object, it is automatically `JSON.stringify`ed.
175: 
176: 
177: 
178: ### async copy (*src*) .to (...*dst*) {.method}
179: 
180: Copies `src` to `dst`, optionally with a fluent API. Both can be files or folders.
181: 
182: ```js
183: const { copy } = cds.utils
184: await copy('db/data').to('dist','db','data')
185: await copy('db/data').to('dist/db/data')
186: await copy('db/data','dist/db/data')
187: ```
188: 
189: The implementation essentially uses `fs.promises.cp()`, with relative fileames resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).
190:

193: ### async mkdirp (...*path*) {.method}
194: 
195: Creates a directory at the given path.
196: 
197: ```js
198: const { mkdirp } = cds.utils
199: await mkdirp('dist','db','data')
200: await mkdirp('dist/db/data')
201: ```
202: 
203: The implementation essentially uses `fs.promises.mkdir(...,{recursive:true})`, with relative fileames resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).
204: 
205: 
206: 
207: ### async rmdir (...*path*) {.method}
208: 
209: Deletes the *directory* at the given path, throwing an error if it doesn't exist.
210: 
211: ```js
212: const { rmdir } = cds.utils
213: await rmdir('dist','db','data')
214: await rmdir('dist/db/data')
215: ```
216: 
217: The implementation essentially uses `fs.promises.rm(...,{recursive:true})`, with relative fileames resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).
218: 
219: 
220: 
221: ### async rimraf (...*path*) {.method}
222: 
223: Deletes the *directory* at the given path, if exists, doing nothing, if not.
224: 
225: ```js
226: const { rimraf } = cds.utils
227: await rimraf('dist','db','data')
228: await rimraf('dist/db/data')
229: ```
230: 
231: The implementation essentially uses `fs.promises.mkdir(...,{recursive:true, force:true})`, with relative fileames resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).
232: 
233: 
234: 
235: ### async rm (...*path*) {.method}
236: 
237: Deletes the *file* at the given path.
238: 
239: ```js
240: const { rm } = cds.utils
241: await rm('dist','db','data')
242: await rm('dist/db/data')
243: ```
244: 
245: The implementation essentially uses `fs.promises.rm()`, with relative fileames resolved in relation to [`cds.root`](cds-facade#cds-root).

249: 
250: Provides utilities for coloring terminal output. Colors are automatically enabled if the terminal supports it, but can be overridden via environment variables `NO_COLOR` or `FORCE_COLOR`.

254: console.log(BRIGHT, RED, 'this is bright red text', RESET)

256: ```

      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

SYNOPSIS

  cds-typer [cds file | "*"]

  Generates type information based on a CDS model.
  Call with at least one positional parameter pointing
  to the (root) CDS file you want to compile.

OPTIONS

  --buildTask
  --build_task: <true | false>
    (default: true)

    If set to true, the typescript build task will not be registered/ executed.
    This value must be set in your project configuration.
    Passing it as parameter to the cds-typer CLI has no effect.

  --brandedPrimitiveTypes
  --branded_primitive_types: <true | false>
    (default: false)

    If set to true, generated primitive types will be branded to prevent accidental mixing of types with the same underlying primitive.
    E.g., type CustomerID = string & { __brand: 'CustomerID' }

  --cache: <none | blake2s256>
    (default: none)

    How to cache typer runs.
    none: fully run cds-typer whenever it is called
    blake2s256: only run if the blake2s256-hash of the model has changed. Hash is stored in a file between runs.

  --help

    This text.

  --inlineDeclarations
  --inline_declarations: <flat | structured>
    (default: flat)

    Whether to resolve inline type declarations
    flat: (x_a, x_b, ...)
    or structured: (x: {a, b}).

  --IEEE754Compatible
  --ieee754compatible: <true | false>
    (default: false)

    If set to true, floating point properties are generated
    as IEEE754 compatible '(number | string)' instead of 'number'.

  --jsConfigPath
  --js_config_path: <string>

    Path to where the jsconfig.json should be written.
    If specified, cds-typer will create a jsconfig.json file and
    set it up to restrict property usage in types entities to
    existing properties only.

  --logLevel
  --log_level SILENT | ERROR | WARN | INFO | DEBUG | TRACE | SILLY | VERBOSE
    (default: ERROR)

    Minimum log level that is printed.
    The default is only used if no explicit value is passed
    and there is no configuration passed via cds.env either.

  --legacyBinaryTypes
  --legacy_binary_types: <true | false>
    (default: false)

    If set to true, Binary and LargeBinary are generated
    as strings.

  --outputDirectory
  --output_directory: <string>
    (default: ./)

    Root directory to write the generated files to.
